# Abstract

Between the close of the Younger Dryas cold stadial in 10000BC and the establishment of Early Neolithic farming across the Aegean, Balkans and Lower Danube by 6000BC, the human population of Europe outside the eastern steppes expanded nearly fivefold. Across 12 biophysical sub-regions spanning 7.148.884 km² (of which 5.072.076 km² lay outside the glaciated Greenland and High Arctic zone), aggregate population grew from 217,1k (217.100, including 215,1k across ten temperate, Mediterranean and Baltic basins plus a 2k nominal coastal floor along the North Atlantic margins) in 10000BC to 442k (442.000) in 8000BC and reached 1,04M (1.036.000) by 6000BC [@BocquetAppel2005; @Tallavaara2015; @Zimmermann2009]. At the opening of the Holocene, 70,9% of Europe's inhabitants remained concentrated in the southern glacial refugia of Iberia (56k), Franco-Aquitaine (54k) and Italy (44k), where Late Magdalenian, Azilian and Epigravettian bands sustained densities of 0,09 to 0,125 inhabitants per km² [@MaierZimmermann2017; @Shao2025Pathways]. Rapid Preboreal and Boreal warming opened Britain, the Low Countries, the North European Plain and deglaciating Fennoscandia, lifting mean density across inhabited Europe from 0,043 inhabitants per km² in 10000BC to 0,2 inhabitants per km² in 6000BC while eustatic sea-level rise drowned Doggerland and separated Britain from the continent [@Tallavaara2015; @Kelm2023Retold]. By 6000BC, regional densities diverged across nearly two orders of magnitude: the Balkan-Lower Danube and Aegean corridor led decisively at 390k inhabitants (0,75 inhabitants per km², 37,6% of all Europe) as cereal farming spread across Thessaly and Thrace, followed by Italy (155k, 0,41 inhabitants per km²), the Carpathian and Middle Danube basin (108k, 0,29 inhabitants per km²) and the richest pre-agrarian wetland estuary of Rhine-Meuse (44k, 0,24 inhabitants per km²), down to 0,025 inhabitants per km² across boreal Fennoscandia [@Pinhasi2005; @Shennan2013; @Timpson2014]. This study calibrates regional headcounts across all 12 sub-regions against radiocarbon summed probability distributions, ecological carrying capacities and a gazetteer of 1.846 catalogued habitation locales led by 1.814 radiocarbon-dated European archaeological sites and 14 scholarly prehistory benchmarks.

# Background

## Glacial Refugia and the Late Pleistocene Demographic Floor

Modern human settlement in Europe during the Late Pleistocene was governed directly by ice-sheet geometry, permafrost margins and the seasonal carrying capacity of mammoth-steppe tundra [@BocquetAppel2005; @Tallavaara2015]. Long before the Holocene opened, anatomical and behavioural turnover during the Middle to Upper Palaeolithic transition had replaced sparse Neanderthal bands with Aurignacian and Gravettian hunter-gatherers organised into wider regional mating and exchange networks [@Villa2014Neandertal; @Gabora2013Contextual; @Bicho2017Early; @Schmidt2019Population]. Even at the Gravettian height around 27000BC, western and central Europe north of the Alps probably held no more than a few thousand people dispersed along loess corridors and river valleys [@MaierZimmermann2017; @Nett2021Early].

When the Last Glacial Maximum peaked between 24000BC and 18000BC, the Fennoscandian ice cap covered Scandinavia, the Baltic basin, Scotland and northern England, while Alpine glaciers sealed off the central mountain passes. Continuous permafrost extended across southern Britain, the Low Countries, northern France and the North European Plain down to the 46th parallel [@Tallavaara2015]. Human settlement north of the Loire and the Middle Danube effectively collapsed, driving surviving bands southward into three primary Mediterranean-Atlantic refugia: the Iberian-Cantabrian littoral and southwestern France (Franco-Cantabria), the Italian peninsula with its expanded Adriatic plain and the Balkan-Aegean valleys bordering the Lower Danube [@BocquetAppel2005; @Shao2025Pathways; @MaierZimmermann2017].

Within these refugia, demographic survival hinged on topographic diversity. Steep elevation gradients in Cantabria, the Pyrenees, the Apennines and the Pindus allowed small mobile bands of 25 to 50 people to move seasonally between coastal marine shelves, wooded foothills and upland ibex or chamois pastures without crossing sterile ice-margin deserts [@Shao2025Pathways; @Domingo2023Nuevo]. Yet even inside the richest shelters of Périgord and Asturias, population remained thin. Local band extinctions were frequent whenever harsh winters interrupted migratory herd routes, forcing surviving groups to rely on long-distance kin ties to replenish demographic shortfalls [@Premo2010Modeling; @Blythe2006Propagation].

## Late Glacial Recolonisation: Magdalenian, Azilian and Federmesser Expansion

Retreat of the continental ice sheets after 16000BC initiated the first sustained northward recolonisation of Europe. From the Franco-Cantabrian core, Late Magdalenian reindeer hunters moved up the Loire and Seine into the Paris Basin, crossed the Ardennes into the Meuse valley (where stratified cave sequences such as Scladina document long-term Pleistocene occupation cycles) and advanced into the Upper Rhine, Swabian Jura and Moravia [@Vonhof2024Improving; @Tallavaara2015; @BocquetAppel2005]. During the Bølling-Allerød interstadial (12700BC to 10900BC), mean July temperatures rose sharply across western Europe, drawing pioneer Creswellian and Federmesser groups across the dry English Channel river valley into southern Britain and eastward onto the sandy outwash plains of the Elbe and Oder.

That expansion suffered an abrupt climatic reverse during the Younger Dryas stadial (10900BC to 9600BC). Within a few decades, North Atlantic cooling restored tundra conditions from Ireland to Poland, pushing treeline boundaries southward and thinning northern horse and red deer herds. Specialised open-country hunters of the Ahrensburgian and Swiderian traditions tracked migratory reindeer across the North European Plain, while southern groups in Iberia, Aquitaine and Italy adapted under Azilian and Late Epigravettian lithic industries [@Tallavaara2015; @Domingo2023Nuevo].

Our earliest benchmark of 10000BC sits near the closing centuries of the Younger Dryas, just before the abrupt Preboreal warming of 9600BC. At that moment Europe's human geography still mirrored the ice-age map. Out of an estimated 217,1k inhabitants across the study domain (215,1k across the ten continental and insular basins plus a 2k nominal coastal floor along the North Atlantic margins, with Greenland uninhabited), 154k (70,9% of the domain total, or 71,6% excluding the boreal margin floor) lived in the three southern refugia of Iberia (56k), Franco-Aquitaine (54k) and Italy (44k). Another 24k inhabited the Balkan-Aegean zone, 11k occupied the Rhine-Meuse valley and 10k lived in the Alpine and Upper Danube foothills. North and east of those temperate corridors, settlement remained exceptionally thin: 7,5k across the North European Plain, 5,5k in the Carpathian and Middle Danube basin, 2,5k on the British-Irish shelf and barely 600 pioneer hunters along the ice-free fringes of southern Fennoscandia.

## Post-Glacial Sea-Level Rise and the Submergence of Doggerland

The warming that began around 9600BC transformed both the ecology and the coastline of Europe. As the Laurentide and Fennoscandian ice sheets melted, global sea level climbed rapidly from roughly 60 m below modern datum at 10000BC to within 10 m of present levels by 6000BC. Across northwestern and southern Europe, vast low-lying plains that had supported prime riverine foraging habitats vanished beneath the sea.

Nowhere was this territorial loss more consequential than in the southern North Sea basin. At 10000BC and 8000BC, Doggerland formed an undulating landscape of chalk hills, braided estuaries, freshwater meres and reed marshes linking eastern England directly to Denmark and the Netherlands. Early Mesolithic hunter-gatherers walked unimpeded from Yorkshire to Jutland, exploiting pike, waterfowl, elk and red deer across wetlands far richer than the drier upland heaths that survived later inundation [@Kelm2023Retold; @Tallavaara2015]. Similar lowland losses occurred in the northern Adriatic, where rising seas flooded the Great Adriatic Plain south of the Po delta, and across the Aegean Sea, where land bridges fractured into the Cycladic islands.

Between 7500BC and 6200BC, encroaching tides severed the chalk ridge of the Strait of Dover and turned Dogger Bank into a shrinking low island. Around 6200BC, two rapid shocks coincided: the final drainage of glacial Lake Agassiz triggered a century-long cold spell across the North Atlantic, and the Storegga submarine landslide off western Norway drove tsunami waves across the low-lying remnants of Doggerland, the Scottish coast and the Norwegian littoral. Britain became an island, Ireland had already been isolated for millennia and displaced coastal bands compressed into the estuaries of the Rhine, Meuse, Scheldt, Thames and Danish fjords. That wetland enrichment and coastal compression explains why the Rhine-Meuse and Low Countries sub-region led all of Europe in density during the 8000BC Boreal peak (0,2 inhabitants per km²) and remained Europe's densest strictly pre-agrarian landscape by 6000BC at 0,24 inhabitants per km² across its terrestrial footprint of 182.447 km².

## Boreal Forest Closure, Aquatic Intensification and the Aegean Neolithic Threshold

As warming progressed through the Preboreal (9600BC to 8500BC) and Boreal (8500BC to 6800BC) chronozones, open birch-pine parkland gave way to dense temperate woodlands dominated by hazel, oak, elm, lime and alder. For hunters accustomed to stalking open-steppe herds, forest closure posed an ecological challenge: terrestrial ungulate biomass became more dispersed and harder to intercept, shifting subsistence from migratory reindeer to solitary woodland mammals such as red deer, roe deer, aurochs and wild boar [@Tallavaara2015; @Zimmermann2009].

Mesolithic communities answered forest closure with technological miniaturisation and aquatic intensification. Composite microlithic arrows, dug-out canoes, woven fish traps, barbed bone harpoons and domestic dogs enabled bands to harvest high-yield coastal, lacustrine and riverine niches [@Kelm2023Retold]. In Atlantic Iberia, Late Mesolithic groups built large seasonal shell-midden aggregations along the Tagus and Sado estuaries, exemplified by Cabeço da Amoreira, alongside deeply stratified Cantabrian caves such as El Mirón and interior Spanish rock shelters tracking upland wild game and hazel groves [@Domingo2023Nuevo]. Along the Danube Iron Gates gorge, communities at Lepenski Vir, Padina, Schela Cladovei and Vlasac constructed trapezoidal semi-subterranean dwellings overlooking sturgeon-rich rapids, achieving near-sedentary village scale without domesticated cereals. Across the northern lowlands, wetland stations such as Verrebroeck in the Scheldt basin, Friesack and Duvensee on the North European Plain and Tågerup, Skateholm and Zvejnieki around the Baltic anchored intensive fishing and fowling economies.

Across western and central Europe, ancient DNA confirms that these Mesolithic populations belonged largely to a genetically cohesive Western Hunter-Gatherer (WHG) metapopulation, exemplified by the skeleton from Abri Loschbour in Luxembourg (c. 6000BC), which remained distinct from Eastern and Scandinavian hunter-gatherers until the arrival of Anatolian-derived farmers [@Haak2015; @Olalde2018]. Along the northeastern forest fringe and eastern Baltic, Late Mesolithic foragers even began adopting early hunter-gatherer pottery traditions diffusing westward across Eurasia well before agriculture reached the boreal zone [@Pavlu2019Earliest].

In southeastern Europe, however, the demographic regime changed fundamentally before our closing horizon of 6000BC. Farming groups carrying domesticated einkorn, emmer wheat, barley, sheep, goats and cattle crossed from western Anatolia into the Aegean basin around 6800BC to 6500BC, establishing permanent mudbrick tell settlements across Thessaly, Macedonia, Crete and Thrace, led in our site register by Sesklo, Karanovo, Dikili Tash, Knossos, Nea Nikomedeia, Argissa Magoula, Achilleion and Anzabegovo alongside long-occupied coastal caves such as Franchthi Cave and Theopetra Cave [@Pinhasi2005; @Shennan2013]. Because cereal cultivation and stock-raising supported five to ten times more people per square kilometre than broad-spectrum foraging, the Balkan-Lower Danube and Aegean sub-region surged more than sixfold from 62k inhabitants in 8000BC to 390k in 6000BC (0,75 inhabitants per km²), accounting for 37,6% of Europe's entire population at the close of the Mesolithic era [@Pinhasi2005; @Timpson2014].

# Methodology

## Biophysical Partition of the Twelve Sub-Regions

To track demographic redistribution across sharp climatic, glacial and coastal gradients without forcing prehistoric populations into anachronistic modern state borders, MAGNETIC partitions Europe and the North Atlantic into 12 biophysical sub-regions totalling 7.148.884,3 km². Because Greenland and the High Arctic account for 2.076.808,1 km² of glaciated and polar terrain that remained entirely uninhabited prior to Palaeo-Eskimo arrival around 2500BC, all demographic density comparisons distinguish between the full continental-arctic domain (7,15M km²) and the inhabited European landmass (5.072.076,2 km²).

The 12 territorial divisions group coherent river basins, mountain watersheds and marine shelves:

1. Southern Mediterranean-Atlantic refugia: Iberian-Cantabrian Refugium (623.682,3 km²), Italian Peninsula and Po Basin (379.386 km²) and Balkan-Lower Danube and Aegean (519.757,1 km²).
2. Temperate western basins and shelves: Franco-Aquitaine and Loire Basins (432.028,6 km²), Rhine-Meuse and Low Countries (182.446,9 km²) and British-Irish Insular Shelf (311.645,6 km²).
3. Central European watersheds and lowlands: Alpine and Upper Danube-Rhine (225.245,1 km²), Carpathian and Middle Danube Basin (376.443 km²) and North European Plain from the Elbe through the Oder and Vistula (616.194,3 km²).
4. Boreal and Arctic frontiers: Fennoscandian Shield and Baltic (1.303.262,9 km²), North Atlantic Boreal Margins covering outer boreal coasts and Atlantic islands (101.984,7 km²) and Greenland and High Arctic (2.076.808,1 km²).

This regional architecture aligns directly with palaeoclimatic pollen zones and radiocarbon clusters, allowing separate tracking of LGM refugial persistence, northern deglaciation lags and the 6000BC southeastern agrarian frontier [@Tallavaara2015; @Pinhasi2005].

## Radiocarbon Calibration and Carrying-Capacity Estimation

Prehistoric hunter-gatherers left no tax rolls, hearth counts or administrative censuses. Regional population totals $P_r(t)$ at the three benchmark years $t \in \{-10000, -8000, -6000\}$ are therefore reconstructed by triangulating three independent lines of evidence: calibrated radiocarbon summed probability distributions (SPDs), archaeological site-catchment density models and ecological carrying-capacity bounds [@BocquetAppel2005; @Zimmermann2009; @Timpson2014; @Shennan2013].

For each sub-region $r$ of terrestrial area $A_r$, regional population is expressed through its effective ecological density $d_r(t)$:

$$P_r(t) = A_r \cdot d_r(t)$$

where $d_r(t)$ is constrained between observed ethnographic and archaeological limits for temperate-to-boreal hunter-gatherers (0,0005 to 0,25 inhabitants per km² prior to cereal farming, rising to 0,29 to 0,75 inhabitants per km² along the 6000BC Early Neolithic agrarian arc) and modulated longitudinally by regional radiocarbon intensity [@BocquetAppel2005; @Zimmermann2009; @Schmidt2019Population]. Specifically, if $S_r(t)$ denotes the bias-corrected radiocarbon activity index for sub-region $r$ within a 500-year window centred on benchmark $t$, the inter-benchmark growth ratio satisfies:

$$\frac{P_r(t_2)}{P_r(t_1)} = \left(\frac{S_r(t_2)}{S_r(t_1)}\right)^{\beta_r} \cdot \phi_r(t_1, t_2)$$

where $\beta_r \in [0,6, 0,85]$ dampens raw radiocarbon surge bias caused by taphonomic preservation decay and modern excavation clustering, and $\phi_r(t_1, t_2)$ incorporates palaeoenvironmental habitat expansion (ice-sheet retreat in Fennoscandia and the British-Irish shelf) or coastal contraction (Doggerland drowning) [@Tallavaara2015; @Timpson2014]. Compound annual growth rates between benchmarks follow standard geometric compounding:

$$g_r(t_1, t_2) = \left(\frac{P_r(t_2)}{P_r(t_1)}\right)^{\frac{1}{t_2 - t_1}} - 1$$

Because hunter-gatherer populations operate near local carrying capacity with frequent stochastic band extinctions and re-fusions, long-run prehistoric growth rates inside settled refugia stay very low, typically 0,01% to 0,02% per annum, corresponding to doubling times of 3.000 to 6.000 years [@Premo2010Modeling; @Blythe2006Propagation]. Departures far above 0,04% per annum mark distinct ecological shifts: either pioneer colonisation of newly deglaciated virgin territory (as in Britain and Fennoscandia between 10000BC and 8000BC) or the introduction of domesticated cereals and livestock (as in the 6000BC Aegean, Balkans and Carpathian basin) [@Pinhasi2005; @Shennan2013].

## Site Gazetteer Assembly and Provenance Architecture

Alongside macro-regional population totals, MAGNETIC compiles a spatially referenced gazetteer of 1.846 catalogued habitation locales distributed across 41 modern national territories. Primary archaeological ingestion (Wave 1) assembled 1.828 entries (99,02% of the gazetteer), combining 1.814 radiocarbon-dated European cave, rock-shelter, shell-midden and open-air camp sites from the European Radiocarbon Settlement Corpus (98,27%) with 14 Scholarly European Prehistory Benchmarks (0,76%) anchoring major Early Neolithic tell settlements and Mesolithic type sites. Spatial deduplication against 2.611 candidate records eliminated 765 redundant trench names, sub-stratigraphic duplicates and overlapping coordinates within narrow local buffers.

In addition, Wave 4 regional continuity sweeps retained 18 geographical anchor points (0,98%) across the North Atlantic and Greenland: 7 in Greenland (4 from national statistical registers and 3 from GeoNames), 10 in the Faroe Islands (4 from national statistical registers and 6 from GeoNames) and 1 in Iceland from Buringh's European urban baseline, holding the overall crowd-sourced share to 0,49% (9 of 1.846 entries). Those 18 nodes serve strictly as cross-chapter geographic continuity markers for the multi-millennium MAGNETIC pipeline. Greenland's prehistoric regional headcount remains strictly zero across 10000BC, 8000BC and 6000BC, and the North Atlantic Boreal Margins series (assigned a 2k nominal maritime-margin floor in 10000BC against 0 raw pre-Boreal inland count, 2k in 8000BC and 4k in 6000BC) reflects marine foraging along ice-free outer Norwegian and northern Scottish coasts rather than pre-Norse occupation of Iceland or the Faroes.

Because prehistoric strata lack historical census rolls, individual locales are scaled along a continuous archaeologically calibrated size distribution governed by regional ecological productivity, chronological phase and radiocarbon occupation intensity [@Schmidt2019Population; @Zimmermann2009]. Estimated site sizes span smoothly from small mobile Palaeolithic and Mesolithic foraging camps (20 to 75 people, typically represented by single or few radiocarbon dates in northern and upland settings), through recurrent seasonal base camps (75 to 180 people) and multi-phase coastal, estuarine and riverine aggregation complexes (180 to 450 people, including Arene Candide, Schela Cladovei, Lepenski Vir, Franchthi Cave, Padina, Verrebroeck and Cabeço da Amoreira), up to the first permanent Early Neolithic agro-pastoral tell villages of the 6500BC to 6000BC Aegean-Balkan threshold (440 to 1.450 inhabitants, led by Sesklo at 1.450, Karanovo at 820 and Dikili Tash at 773).

# Validation

## Cross-Checks Against Palaeodemographic Benchmarks

To check that regional estimates remain tightly bounded within established palaeodemographic consensus, MAGNETIC continental totals and densities were cross-checked against four independent archaeological syntheses. For the Late Upper Palaeolithic (Magdalenian, c. 14000BC to 11000BC), Bocquet-Appel and colleagues estimated a European meta-population of roughly 29k to 40k across core western and central archaeologically surveyed regions, scaling upward substantially once southern Mediterranean refugia, the Balkans and coastal plains are included [@BocquetAppel2005]. Using bioclimatic envelope modelling across Europe, Tallavaara and colleagues reconstructed a Last Glacial Maximum low of approximately 130k people around 21000BC, expanding to roughly 330k to 410k during the Late Glacial warming peak before dipping during the Younger Dryas cold stadial [@Tallavaara2015].

Our 10000BC domain figure of 217,1k (215,1k across the ten continental and insular sub-regions) captures that Younger Dryas contraction directly. Equally important, the implied mean density across inhabited Europe in 10000BC (0,043 inhabitants per km², ranging from 0,09 to 0,125 in the three southern refugia down to 0,0005 in southern Fennoscandia) matches the archaeological density envelope derived by Schmidt and Zimmermann for Upper Palaeolithic core catchments (0,01 to 0,15 inhabitants per km² depending on regional productivity) [@Schmidt2019Population; @MaierZimmermann2017].

By 6000BC, inhabited European density reaches 0,2 inhabitants per km², concealing a sharp ecological bifurcation. Strictly pre-agrarian foraging regions span 0,025 inhabitants per km² in boreal Fennoscandia and 0,06 in the closed woodlands of the North European Plain up to 0,18 to 0,24 across temperate Atlantic estuaries and river valleys (matching Zimmermann, Hilpert and Wendt's comparative pre-Neolithic range of 0,05 to 0,25 inhabitants per km²), while the Early Neolithic farming arc already climbs to 0,29 in the Carpathian basin, 0,41 in Italy and 0,75 in the Balkan-Lower Danube and Aegean, entering the lower threshold of mature Linearbandkeramik (LBK) agrarian densities (0,6 to 2 inhabitants per km²) that emerged north of the Balkans after 5500BC [@Zimmermann2009; @Shennan2013].

</figure>

Across the four millennia from 10000BC to 6000BC, overall continental growth averaged 0,039% per annum (0,036% from 10000BC to 8000BC and 0,043% from 8000BC to 6000BC, a 4,77-fold expansion). The two westernmost Late Glacial refugia grew at the slowest proportional rates, 1,59x in Franco-Aquitaine and 2x in Iberia, because they opened the Holocene closest to their foraging carrying capacity. By contrast, newly deglaciated northern zones expanded far faster from minimal Younger Dryas baselines: 53,33x in Fennoscandia and the Baltic (from 600 to 32k) and 15,2x across the British-Irish shelf (from 2,5k to 38k, almost all gained during the Preboreal-Boreal surge before 8000BC). In southeastern Europe, an altogether different acceleration took hold after 8000BC: the Carpathian and Middle Danube basin expanded 19,64x overall (4,5x in the final two millennia alone) and the Balkan-Lower Danube and Aegean surged 16,25x overall (multiplying 6,29x between 8000BC and 6000BC, from 62k to 390k), registering the unmistakable demographic break of the Early Neolithic transition [@Pinhasi2005; @Shennan2013].

# Results

## Continental Demographic Trajectory (10000BC to 6000BC)

Europe's prehistoric demographic curve from 10000BC to 6000BC exhibits two distinct phases of expansion: a Preboreal-Boreal northward recolonisation followed by a sharp southeastern agrarian surge (Figure \ref{fig:palaeo-trajectory}). Between 10000BC and 8000BC, aggregate population rose by 224,9k (+103,59%) from 217,1k to 442k. Between 8000BC and 6000BC, it added a further 594k (+134,39%) to reach 1.036.000 (1,04M) inhabitants, crossing the one-million mark for the first time in European prehistory.

<figure class="crd-figure-block" id="fig:palaeo-trajectory">
<img class="crd-figure-img" src="/artefacts/project_magnetic/1.0-prehistoric-palaeolithic-mesolithic-europe/prehistoric_palaeolithic_mesolithic_europe_population_trajectory.png" alt="fig:palaeo-trajectory" loading="lazy" />
<figcaption class="crd-caption"><span class="crd-caption-label">Figure 2.</span> Aggregate demographic trajectory for Europe and its four largest sub-regions from 10000BC to 6000BC (Panel A) and sub-regional population density rankings in 6000BC (Panel B).</figcaption>
</figure>

Even more revealing than the headline total is the internal redistribution of Europe's population. In 10000BC, the three Western Mediterranean and Atlantic refugia (Iberia, Franco-Aquitaine and Italy) accounted for 70,9% of all European inhabitants (154k of 217,1k), while temperate central and northern Europe (Britain, Low Countries, Alpine-Upper Danube, North European Plain, Fennoscandia and North Atlantic margins) held only 15,5% (33,6k) and the Danubian-Balkan-Aegean axis held 13,6% (29,5k). By 8000BC, Preboreal-Boreal warming had transformed the northwest: temperate central and northern Europe more than doubled its share to 32,6% (144k), reducing the western refugia to 48% (212k) while the southeastern axis rose to 19,5% (86k). By 6000BC, the balance tilted dramatically southeastward: the Danubian-Balkan-Aegean corridor accounted for 48,1% of Europe's population (37,6% in the Balkan-Aegean alone plus 10,4% in the Carpathian and Middle Danube basin), the three western refugia represented 34,1% (bolstered by Italy's rise to 15% on the Apulian Neolithic threshold) and strictly pre-agrarian central and northern Europe accounted for 17,9% (185k).

## Southern Refugia and the Mediterranean-Atlantic Core

The Iberian-Cantabrian Refugium (623.682,3 km²) opened the Holocene as Europe's largest demographic reservoir at 56k inhabitants (0,09 inhabitants per km²), expanding steadily to 78k in 8000BC (0,125 inhabitants per km²) and 112k in 6000BC (0,18 inhabitants per km²). Iberia supplies the second-largest regional share of our archaeological gazetteer with 297 catalogued sites (205 in Spain, 61 in Portugal, 3 in Andorra and 1 in Gibraltar, plus 27 Pyrenean-margin sites in southern France). Settlement was strongly polarised between two ecological strips: the wet Atlantic-Cantabrian facade and the Mediterranean karst valleys of the Ebro and Levant, separated by the drier interior Meseta [@Shao2025Pathways; @Domingo2023Nuevo]. Along the Cantabrian cordillera and Pyrenees, deeply stratified caves and rock shelters such as El Mirón sustained recurring seasonal camps across the Azilian and Asturian transitions, while along the Tagus and Sado estuaries of Portugal, major shell-midden complexes exemplified by Cabeço da Amoreira anchored intensive Late Mesolithic foraging that persisted until Cardial Neolithic pioneers sailed westward along the Mediterranean rim after 5800BC [@Bicho2017Early; @Shao2025Pathways].

Immediately across the Pyrenees, the Franco-Aquitaine and Loire Basins (432.028,6 km²) held Europe's highest regional density at the opening of the Holocene: 54k inhabitants in 10000BC (0,125 inhabitants per km²), rising modestly to 68k in 8000BC (0,157 inhabitants per km²) and 86k in 6000BC (0,2 inhabitants per km²), documented across 245 catalogued sites. Inheriting the dense Magdalenian networks of the Dordogne, Vézère, Lot and Garonne valleys, Azilian and Sauveterrian foragers spread northward across the Loire and Seine catchments into wooded river valleys and sandy uplands. Even as northern France transitioned into closed Boreal oak-hazel forest, Aquitaine and the Brittany coast retained rich salmon rivers and marine estuaries capable of sustaining durable Mesolithic communities.

Across the Alps, the Italian Peninsula and Po Basin (379.386 km²) stood close behind at 44k in 10000BC (0,116 inhabitants per km²), rising to 66k in 8000BC (0,174 inhabitants per km²) before accelerating to 155k in 6000BC (0,41 inhabitants per km², second highest in Europe), supported by 198 catalogued sites. Late Epigravettian and Sauveterrian groups across Sicily, Liguria (anchored by the long stratigraphic sequence at Arene Candide, peaking at 542 inhabitants), Tuscany, the Tyrrhenian lagoons (Portus Fiumicino, 418) and the Alpine piedmont adapted smoothly to Holocene warming, moving into high summer hunting camps in the Dolomites and Trentino as snowlines retreated. Although rising Adriatic waters flooded the wide glacial plain southeast of Venice, the fertile Po river terraces and southern Apulian coasts sustained vigorous growth, and by 6000BC Apulia and southeastern Italy had crossed the threshold of Impressed Ware maritime farming from across the Strait of Otranto [@Pinhasi2005].

## Balkan-Aegean Expansion and Danubian Corridors

The single greatest demographic transformation of the 10000BC to 6000BC epoch unfolded in the Balkan-Lower Danube and Aegean sub-region (519.757,1 km²). At 10000BC, its 24k inhabitants (0,046 inhabitants per km²) trailed Iberia, Franco-Aquitaine and Italy by a wide margin, and at 8000BC its 62k inhabitants (0,119 inhabitants per km²) still sat below those three western basins. Between 8000BC and 6000BC, however, the region surged more than sixfold to 390k inhabitants (0,75 inhabitants per km²), overtaking every other part of Europe by a factor of two and a half and accounting for 37,6% of the continental total.

Two distinct processes drove this surge, both recorded across the sub-region's 129 catalogued sites (led by 63 in Greece, 17 in Serbia, 12 in Bulgaria, 7 in Bosnia and Herzegovina, 6 in Montenegro, 3 each in Albania and European Turkey and 2 in North Macedonia, plus adjacent Lower Danubian stations in Romania and Moldova). First, in the Iron Gates gorges of the Lower Danube, complex Mesolithic fishing communities at Schela Cladovei (441), Padina (409), Lepenski Vir (394) and Vlasac (340) achieved semi-sedentary village density by exploiting migrating beluga sturgeon and carp along rocky river narrows. Second, and decisively, Anatolian farming populations established permanent agro-pastoral tell villages across Thessaly, Macedonia, Crete and Thrace, led in our catalogue by Sesklo (1.450), Karanovo (820), Dikili Tash (773), Knossos (680), Nea Nikomedeia (620), Argissa Magoula (540), Achilleion (490) and Anzabegovo (440) alongside long-occupied coastal and inland caves such as Franchthi Cave (418) and Theopetra Cave (419) [@Pinhasi2005; @Shennan2013]. Unlike hunter-gatherers bound by seasonal resource troughs, early farmers stored cereal grain over winter, shortened birth intervals and sustained rapid local population doubling [@BocquetAppel2005; @Timpson2014].

Upstream along the Danube, the Carpathian and Middle Danube Basin (376.443 km²) expanded from a sparse Younger Dryas baseline of 5,5k in 10000BC (0,015 inhabitants per km²) to 24k in 8000BC (0,064 inhabitants per km²) before jumping 4,5-fold to 108k in 6000BC (0,29 inhabitants per km², third highest in Europe). Although deep Holocene alluvial burial across the Great Hungarian Plain restricts archaeological recovery to 33 catalogued sites (0,88 sites per 10.000 km², the lowest sampling density of any inhabited temperate basin), Upper Palaeolithic loess sites such as Crvenka-At demonstrate deep Pleistocene continuity along the southern Carpathian rim [@Nett2021Early]. By 6000BC, Early Neolithic Starčevo and Körös farming pioneers were spreading rapidly northward along the Tisza, Maros and Körös rivers, setting the stage for the Linearbandkeramik expansion of the sixth millennium BC [@Pinhasi2005].

To the west, the Alpine and Upper Danube-Rhine sub-region (225.245,1 km²) climbed from 10k in 10000BC (0,044 inhabitants per km²) to 24k in 8000BC (0,107 inhabitants per km²) and 32k in 6000BC (0,14 inhabitants per km²), documented across 88 catalogued sites. As valley glaciers retreated up the Rhône, Rhine, Inn and Upper Danube corridors, post-glacial lakes (Geneva, Neuchâtel, Constance and Federsee) created productive wetland ecotones supporting seasonal movements between winter lakeside fisheries and summer alpine ibex pastures.

## Northwestern Shelves, the Rhine-Meuse Estuary and the North European Plain

North of the Loire and the central European uplands, the Preboreal and Boreal Mesolithic witnessed a rapid filling-in of lowland river basins and maritime estuaries followed by ecological stabilisation once temperate forest closed and rising seas severed Doggerland. The Rhine-Meuse and Low Countries sub-region (182.446,9 km²) grew fourfold from 11k in 10000BC (0,06 inhabitants per km²) to 36k in 8000BC (0,197 inhabitants per km², the highest regional density anywhere in Europe at 8000BC) and 44k in 6000BC (0,24 inhabitants per km², fourth overall and the densest strictly pre-agrarian landscape on the continent). Its 225 catalogued sites (12,33 sites per 10.000 km², led by 109 in the Netherlands and 61 in Belgium, including the major estuarine complex at Verrebroeck at 324 inhabitants, karst caves along the Belgian Meuse and Abri Loschbour in Luxembourg [@Vonhof2024Improving; @Olalde2018]) reflect a landscape uniquely enriched by post-glacial hydrology. As sea level rose across the southern North Sea, river gradients flattened, turning the Rhine-Meuse-Scheldt delta into an expansive mosaic of sandy river dunes (*donken*), tidal creeks, alder carrs and reedbeds teeming with waterfowl, eel, pike, beaver and wild boar. Displaced populations retreating inland from submerged Doggerland augmented local density along this estuary rim.

Across the newly formed English Channel, the British-Irish Insular Shelf (311.645,6 km²) recorded one of Europe's sharpest Early Holocene surges, leaping nearly 13-fold from 2,5k in 10000BC (0,008 inhabitants per km²) to 32k in 8000BC (0,103 inhabitants per km²), before slowing to 38k in 6000BC (0,12 inhabitants per km²) after Doggerland submergence and the Storegga tsunami severed direct continental access. The shelf supplies the single largest regional site count in our gazetteer with 303 catalogued locales (259 in the United Kingdom, 43 in Ireland and 1 on the Isle of Man, led by multi-phase sites such as Hambledon Hill at 431 and Grimes Graves at 341). At 10000BC, human presence was confined to sparse southern English caves and Federmesser camps. By 8000BC, Early Mesolithic Maglemosian-related hunters occupied lakeside base camps across Yorkshire (the Star Carr horizon), the Thames-Kennet valley, Wales and northern England, while pioneer maritime foragers crossed the Irish Sea to colonise Ireland (Mount Sandel horizon) and western Scotland. Following final insular separation around 6200BC, Late Mesolithic Britain and Ireland evolved distinctive narrow-blade microlithic and coastal shell-midden traditions insulated from continental ceramic developments for another two millennia.

East of the Weser, the expansive North European Plain from the Elbe through the Oder and Vistula (616.194,3 km²) surged from 7,5k in 10000BC (0,012 inhabitants per km²) to 34k in 8000BC (0,055 inhabitants per km²) before plateauing at 35k in 6000BC (0,06 inhabitants per km²), anchored by 139 catalogued sites across northern Germany, Denmark and Poland. That near-stagnation between 8000BC and 6000BC reflects classic Boreal forest closure: across the sandy glacial outwash soils of Brandenburg, Pomerania and Masovia, dense closed-canopy oak, lime and elm woodland reduced terrestrial ungulate yields, confining high-density habitation to glacial tunnel valleys, moraine wetlands such as Friesack and Duvensee and western Baltic coastal inlets that laid the foundation for the Ertebølle shell-midden society of the fifth millennium BC [@Kelm2023Retold].

## Deglaciating Boreal Frontiers and the Uninhabited High Arctic

No part of Europe changed its physical geography faster between 10000BC and 6000BC than the Fennoscandian Shield and Baltic sub-region (1.303.262,9 km²). At 10000BC, the remnants of the Scandinavian ice sheet still blanketed central Sweden, Finland and interior Norway, confining barely 600 pioneer hunters (0,0005 inhabitants per km²) to the ice-free western Swedish archipelago, southern Scania and narrow strips of the Norwegian coast (Fosna-Hensbacka and Ahrensburgian traditions). As the ice cap collapsed rapidly during the Preboreal, disappearing from the Swedish interior by 7000BC, post-glacial isostatic rebound lifted new coastal archipelagos out of the Ancylus Lake and early Littorina Sea.

Human groups tracked the retreating ice front at remarkable speed, expanding more than 26-fold to 16k in 8000BC (0,012 inhabitants per km²) and doubling again to 32k in 6000BC (0,025 inhabitants per km², 30 times lower than the contemporary Balkan-Aegean), recorded across 171 catalogued sites (led by 60 in Norway, 43 in Sweden, 15 in Finland and 11 across the Baltic states). Pioneers moving around the ice-free Arctic coast of Norway established the Komsa complex in Finnmark before 9000BC, groups advancing from the southeastern Baltic populated inland Finland (Suomusjärvi culture) and rich coastal stations such as Tågerup, Skateholm and Zvejnieki supported substantial Late Mesolithic cemeteries and seasonal villages around the Baltic littoral. Even at 6000BC, however, boreal conifer forests imposed strict winter calorie bottlenecks, keeping overall shield density at 0,025 inhabitants per km² and tying most settlements to coastal seal hunting, salmon rivers and lake outlets.

Along the exposed North Atlantic Boreal Margins (101.984,7 km²), encompassing outer fjordic western and northern Norway and the northernmost Atlantic boreal fringe, the harmonised benchmark series registers 2k in 10000BC (a nominal coastal continuity floor against zero raw inland pre-Boreal signal), 2k in 8000BC (0,02 inhabitants per km²) and 4k in 6000BC (0,04 inhabitants per km²). Warm North Atlantic Drift waters kept outer Norwegian fjords ice-free year-round, supporting marine mammal and cod foraging at densities higher than the interior Fennoscandian Shield. By contrast, Iceland and the Faroe Islands lay beyond the practical open-ocean voyaging horizon of Mesolithic skin boats, and Greenland and the High Arctic (2.076.808,1 km²) remained entirely uninhabited (0 inhabitants) throughout all three benchmarks; human colonisation of Greenland awaited the eastward spread of Arctic Small Tool (Independence I and Saqqaq) Palaeo-Eskimo hunters across the Canadian High Arctic more than three millennia later, around 2500BC.

## Pre-Urban Habitation Structure and Site Distribution

Across Palaeolithic and Mesolithic Europe, residential geography was shaped by small, horizontally linked bands rather than administrative capitals or market towns. By 6000BC, however, the emergence of sedentary agro-pastoral tell villages in the Aegean and Balkans alongside dense estuarine and gorge aggregation sites created an unmistakable continuous settlement-size gradient. Figure \ref{fig:palaeo-hierarchy} displays this structure directly across all 1.846 catalogued habitation records: rather than a steep historical urban Zipf slope ($\alpha \approx 1$), the rank-size curve follows a shallow continuous power law ($\alpha = 0,4$, $R^2 = 0,99$) spanning nearly two orders of magnitude from ephemeral upland foraging camps to permanent Early Neolithic villages.

<img class="crd-figure-img" src="/artefacts/project_magnetic/1.0-prehistoric-palaeolithic-mesolithic-europe/prehistoric_palaeolithic_mesolithic_europe_urban_hierarchy.png" alt="fig:palaeo-hierarchy" loading="lazy" />
<figcaption class="crd-caption"><span class="crd-caption-label">Figure 3.</span> Largest catalogued prehistoric settlements (Panel A) and continuous rank-size distribution across 1.846 habitation sites showing a shallow pre-urban power-law fit ($\alpha = 0,4$, $R^2 = 0,99$, Panel B), 10000BC to 6000BC.</figcaption>
</figure>

At the upper tail of the distribution sit the first permanent Early Neolithic tell settlements of the 6500BC to 6000BC Aegean-Balkan threshold: Sesklo (1.450), Karanovo (820), Dikili Tash (773), Knossos (680), Nea Nikomedeia (620), Argissa Magoula (540), Achilleion (490) and Anzabegovo (440). Immediately beneath them cluster multi-phase karst caves, Iron Gates gorge villages and estuarine aggregation complexes between 180 and 545 inhabitants, including Arene Candide (542), Schela Cladovei (441), Hambledon Hill (431), Eliki (426), Theopetra Cave (419), Franchthi Cave (418), Portus Fiumicino (418), Padina (409), Lepenski Vir (394), Grimes Graves (341), Vlasac (340), Verrebroeck (324) and Cabeço da Amoreira. The middle body of the curve comprises recurrent seasonal Mesolithic base camps (75 to 180 inhabitants), tapering smoothly into hundreds of small mobile Palaeolithic and Mesolithic foraging camps (20 to 75 inhabitants) across northern woodlands and uplands [@Schmidt2019Population; @Premo2010Modeling; @Rowe2019Impact].

Comparing density with site recovery intensity highlights an instructive methodological pattern: the Rhine-Meuse and Low Countries (12,33 sites per 10.000 km²), British-Irish shelf (9,72), Franco-Aquitaine (5,67), Italy (5,22), Iberia (4,76) and Alpine-Upper Danube (3,91) enjoy dense modern rescue archaeology and karst cave preservation, whereas the Carpathian basin (0,88), Fennoscandia (1,31), North European Plain (2,26) and Balkan-Aegean (2,48) suffer far heavier Holocene alluvial burial or lower survey intensity despite very different ecological carrying capacities. Regional headcounts therefore rely on joint bioclimatic and radiocarbon scaling rather than naive raw site summation [@Tallavaara2015; @Timpson2014].

# Limitations

Four structural uncertainties govern prehistoric demographic reconstruction across Palaeolithic and Mesolithic Europe.

First, post-glacial sea-level rise erased Europe's prime coastal foraging landscapes. Between 10000BC and 6000BC, Doggerland, the English Channel valley, the Great Adriatic Plain and substantial sections of the Atlantic and Aegean shelves disappeared beneath marine sediments. Because coastal and estuarine niches typically supported the highest hunter-gatherer densities, terrestrial site catalogues systematically under-sample early littoral populations. Regional totals partially correct for this loss through ecological carrying-capacity bounds, yet the exact headcount displaced from Doggerland into Britain and the Low Countries remains bounded within roughly $\pm 25\%$ [@Tallavaara2015; @Kelm2023Retold].

Second, archaeological visibility varies starkly by geology and modern excavation intensity. Limestone karst regions in Cantabria, Périgord, the Belgian Meuse and the Swiss Jura preserve stratified bone and charcoal in caves and rock shelters [@Vonhof2024Improving; @Domingo2023Nuevo], while waterlogged peat bogs in Denmark and the Netherlands preserve organic wood and bone tools. Conversely, acidic glacial sands on the North European Plain destroy uncharred bone, and thick Holocene river alluvium across the Po, Danube and Tisza basins buries Mesolithic living floors several metres underground [@Nett2021Early]. National survey budgets reinforce these physical differences: France (340 sites), the United Kingdom (259), Spain (205), Italy (140) and Germany (139) together account for 58,7% of the entire gazetteer.

Third, radiocarbon summed probability distributions carry known calibration and dietary biases [@Timpson2014; @Shennan2013]. Atmospheric carbon-14 plateaux during the Younger Dryas and Preboreal compress or stretch apparent site clusters, while freshwater and marine reservoir effects can skew dates on human bone from riverine or coastal fishers by 200 to 500 years unless corrected by stable carbon and nitrogen isotopes. Similarly, while calibrated site-size estimates across all 1.846 locales distinguish permanent Early Neolithic tell villages (440 to 1.450 inhabitants) from seasonal Mesolithic aggregation hubs (180 to 450) and small mobile camps (20 to 75), radiocarbon-derived values for rock shelters and middens still index recurrent seasonal aggregation capacity rather than continuous year-round co-residence [@Schmidt2019Population; @Zimmermann2009].

Fourth, the multi-chapter gazetteer retains 18 Wave-4 spatial anchor records across Greenland (7), the Faroe Islands (10) and Iceland (1) drawn from national statistical and municipal gazetteers to preserve cross-era node continuity across the wider MAGNETIC atlas. Those records carry zero weight in Greenland's regional demographic aggregate (0 inhabitants across all three benchmarks) and do not imply Mesolithic occupation of Iceland or the Faroes.

# Conclusion

Between 10000BC and 6000BC, Europe underwent its first great post-glacial demographic transformation. Driven by rapid Holocene warming, the replacement of tundra by temperate woodlands, the colonisation of deglaciated northern lands and the arrival of cereal agriculture in the southeast, aggregate population expanded nearly fivefold from 217,1k in 10000BC to 442k in 8000BC and 1,04M (1.036.000) in 6000BC. Inhabited European density climbed from 0,043 to 0,2 inhabitants per km² across a continent marked by steep ecological contrasts.

That growth fundamentally rebalanced Europe's human geography. Whereas southern refugia in Iberia, Franco-Aquitaine and Italy held 70,9% of Europe's inhabitants at the close of the Younger Dryas, two millennia of Preboreal and Boreal warming filled Britain, the Rhine-Meuse delta, the North European Plain and deglaciating Fennoscandia. By 6000BC, however, the long equilibrium of European hunter-gatherer demography had broken open. While strictly pre-agrarian regions stabilised between 0,025 inhabitants per km² in boreal Fennoscandia and 0,24 in the Rhine-Meuse wetlands, early agro-pastoral communities along the Aegean littoral and Lower Danube lifted the Balkan-Aegean corridor to 390k inhabitants (0,75 inhabitants per km², 37,6% of all Europe) alongside 155k in Italy and 108k in the Carpathian basin, launching the Neolithic transition that would multiply Europe's population many times over during the millennia ahead [@Pinhasi2005; @Shennan2013; @Haak2015].

## Provenance Corpus Breakdown

Table \ref{tab:provenance-summary} documents the six source corpora contributing to the chapter's settlement register, confirming that 99,02% of catalogued locales derive directly from primary European radiocarbon archaeological inventories (98,27%) and scholarly prehistory benchmarks (0,76%).

<figure class="crd-table-figure" id="tab:provenance-summary">
<div class="crd-table-scroll">
<table class="crd-wysiwyg-table" v-pre>
<thead><tr><th class="crd-th">Source Corpus</th><th class="crd-th">Entries</th><th class="crd-th">Share</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td class="crd-td"><strong>European Radiocarbon Settlement Corpus (Primary Archaeological)</strong></td><td class="crd-td">1.814</td><td class="crd-td">98,27%</td></tr>
<tr><td class="crd-td"><strong>Scholarly European Prehistory Benchmarks (Primary Archaeological)</strong></td><td class="crd-td">14</td><td class="crd-td">0,76%</td></tr>
<tr><td class="crd-td"><strong>GeoNames Municipal Gazetteer Supplement (Arctic/Atlantic Anchors)</strong></td><td class="crd-td">9</td><td class="crd-td">0,49%</td></tr>
<tr><td class="crd-td"><strong>Greenland National Statistical Census (Spatial Continuity Anchors)</strong></td><td class="crd-td">4</td><td class="crd-td">0,22%</td></tr>
